ai.title: Paediatric Neurological Examination
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A systematic bedside approach to assess consciousness, cranial nerves, motor and sensory function, tone, reflexes and coordination in children, adapted for low‑resource settings.

b: Assess level of consciousness, cranial nerves, motor, sensory, tone, reflexes, coordination, gait, and behaviour.
sections.p: The paediatric neurological examination is a structured assessment that localises lesions, grades severity and guides investigations. It is performed after ABCDE and, if the child is unconscious, after rapid screening with AVPU.
Severity is graded using the Pediatric Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and the modified Rankin Scale for functional outcome. Staging of seizures follows the WHO classification (simple, complex, status).

b: Infectious meningitis (bacterial, tubercular), cerebral malaria, neonatal hypoxic‑ischemic encephalopathy, traumatic brain injury, congenital brain malformations, metabolic derangements (hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia).
sections.p: In East Africa the common causes of focal or diffuse neurological deficits are infections (meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral malaria), congenital anomalies, trauma, and metabolic disturbances. Systemic infections such as HIV and TB can also present with neuro‑psychiatric features.

b: Seizure semiology: focal onset, generalized tonic‑clonic, febrile.
sections.p: Children may present with altered consciousness, seizures, focal weakness, abnormal movements, or developmental delay. Behavioural changes, irritability, or failure to thrive may be subtle clues.
When a test is unavailable, use clinical judgment and supportive care; for example, treat suspected bacterial meningitis empirically with ceftriaxone and dexamethasone if possible.

t.b: CSF opening pressure >20 cm H2O, neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein indicates bacterial meningitis; lymphocytes suggest TB or viral. If LP not possible, use bedside ultrasound of optic nerve sheath for raised ICP.
Positive test with neurological signs suggests cerebral malaria.
Cavitary lesions raise suspicion of TB meningitis.

b: Papilledema, sudden loss of consciousness, focal deficits, refractory seizures.
sections.p: Urgent red flags include rapid deterioration, focal neurological signs, seizures, vomiting, papilledema, and signs of raised ICP. Complications can be brain herniation, hydrocephalus, and long‑term neuro‑cognitive deficits.

Treat the underlying cause first: antibiotics for bacterial meningitis, antimalarials for cerebral malaria, antiepileptics for seizures. Supportive care includes airway protection, seizure control, fluid balance, and monitoring for raised ICP.

b: Schedule neuro‑developmental screening at routine well‑child visits.
sections.p: Early rehabilitation, developmental surveillance, and vaccination (Hib, PCV, meningococcal) reduce morbidity. Follow‑up includes neuro‑developmental assessment at 6, 12, and 24 months.

b: Febrile seizures vs. focal seizures; hypoglycaemia vs. meningitis.
sections.p: Seizure disorders can mimic focal deficits; metabolic encephalopathies may present with altered consciousness similar to meningitis.

b: CSF opening pressure may be normal in early disease; repeat LP if high clinical suspicion.
sections.p: Normal CSF glucose can occur in early bacterial meningitis; low protein may be seen in viral infections; optic nerve sheath diameter may be normal in early raised ICP.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe headache with vomiting, sudden loss of consciousness, focal neurological deficit, seizures that do not stop, papilledema, or any sign of raised intracranial pressure.
